stories.headline: JUNE CPI COOLS SHARPLY, FED HOLD ODDS JUMP TO 84.5%
stories.body: Headline CPI rose just 0.4% in June and eased to 3.5% year-over-year, down from May's 4.2% and below the 3.8% consensus; core CPI held at 2.6% YoY. The 10-year yield eased 2 bps to 4.56% and CME FedWatch now prices an 84.5% chance the Fed holds its 3.50%-3.75% range this month.
stories.explain: A 5.7% drop in energy prices, driven by a 9.7% fall in gasoline, did most of the work pulling headline CPI down, while core inflation (which strips out food and energy) barely moved — that's the number the Fed actually weights most heavily when setting policy. Softer core prints reduce the perceived need for further hikes, which is why rate-hold odds jumped and short-end yields eased even as the S&P ground higher on the print.

stories.headline: OIL SURGES AS US-IRAN CONFLICT REIGNITES, HORMUZ BLOCKADE THREATENED
stories.body: WTI jumped roughly 2.4% to around $80, with an intraday high near $81.27 versus Tuesday's $78.14 close, after the administration announced a blockade on Iranian vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz and renewed strikes hit regional energy infrastructure. Brent traded above $85.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz carries roughly a fifth of global oil consumption on tankers passing through a chokepoint only a couple of miles wide at its narrowest — even a partial disruption there tightens seaborne supply immediately, which is why traders price in a risk premium the moment transit is threatened rather than waiting for barrels to actually stop moving. That premium shows up first in the futures curve, not the physical market.

stories.headline: S&P EDGES HIGHER ON CPI RELIEF, NASDAQ SLIPS DESPITE ASML-LED CHIP RALLY
stories.body: The S&P 500 added 0.36% to roughly 7,571 as the cooler CPI print outweighed oil-driven jitters, while the Nasdaq 100 slipped 0.22% to about 29,521 even after ASML lifted its 2026 sales forecast and said it will boost chipmaking-equipment capacity 30% on AI demand.
stories.explain: ASML's forecast raise matters beyond the stock itself because it's a bellwether for capital spending across the entire semiconductor supply chain — when the company that makes the machines chipmakers depend on says demand is accelerating, it signals AI infrastructure spending isn't slowing. The index-level divergence just shows profit-taking in mega-cap tech offsetting that strength elsewhere in the basket.

stories.headline: DOLLAR SLIDES TO SECOND STRAIGHT LOSING SESSION AS RATE-HIKE BETS FADE
stories.body: The DXY dollar index dipped to about 100.78, its second consecutive down session, after the soft CPI report cut the odds of a near-term Fed rate hike. Geopolitical risk from the Iran conflict limited the decline.
stories.explain: The dollar's value is tightly linked to the yield premium US assets offer relative to other currencies — when incoming data lowers the odds of further rate hikes, that expected yield advantage shrinks, and capital flows that had been chasing higher US rates ease off, weakening the currency. Oil-driven safe-haven demand is working in the opposite direction today, which is why the drop is modest rather than sharp.

stories.headline: TEXAS LANDS NO. 1 PROSPECT MARCUS SPEARS JR. IN SURPRISE RECLASSIFICATION
stories.body: Marcus Spears Jr., ranked the No. 1 prospect in the 2027 class, reclassified up and committed to Texas, giving the Longhorns a top-five 2026 class. Because Spears was born in 2009, he'll still need two years in college before he's draft-eligible. Elsewhere, more than 2,700 players moved through the transfer portal in the two-week window after the national title game.

stories.headline: 76ERS PUSH LEBRON PITCH INTO WEEK TWO OF FREE AGENCY
stories.body: Philadelphia is leaning on Tyrese Maxey, Joel Embiid and Jaylen Brown to recruit LeBron James as his free agency search stretches into a second week. Separately, the Kawhi Leonard trade to Toronto remains on hold pending the NBA's outside-counsel investigation, and the Wizards hold the No. 1 pick as their draft plans come into focus.

stories.headline: PACKERS LOCK UP CHRISTIAN WATSON WITH $110.5M EXTENSION
stories.body: Green Bay signed wide receiver Christian Watson to a four-year, $110.5 million extension with a $31 million signing bonus ahead of training camp, which opens for most veterans league-wide on July 24. Titans DT Jeffery Simmons also landed a three-year, $35.3 million-per-year deal making him the highest-paid interior defender in league history.

stories.headline: ACC AND MOUNTAIN WEST OPEN MEDIA DAYS AS MICHIGAN PROBE LOOMS
stories.body: The ACC's three-day Football Kickoff began today in Charlotte with Florida State, Miami, NC State, Stanford and Virginia represented, while Mountain West media days run through Thursday in Las Vegas. Separately, Michigan's board of regents is reviewing a $12 million outside probe into the athletic department's culture, with AD Warde Manuel's job reportedly in question.

sports.detail: On the All-Star break after beating Tampa Bay 8-2 last Sunday behind a Randy Arozarena three-run homer. Sit 2nd in the AL West, one game behind Texas (49-47), and hold a wild-card spot. Return to open the second half Friday vs. the Giants at T-Mobile Park.

Close out 2026 Summer League tonight against Phoenix (6 PM ET, ESPNU) after a 101-93 loss to the 76ers in their opener. No. 17 pick Ebuka Okorie (ex-Stanford) has been the team's top scorer through the tournament. Detroit also acquired Taurean Prince and Gary Harris from Milwaukee for Caris LeVert this month.

The Paul Allen Estate's agreement to sell the franchise to a Khosla family-led group for an NFL-record $9.6 billion still needs ratification from at least 24 of the other 31 owners. Defending Super Bowl champs return 20 of 22 starters; training camp opens July 25 in Renton, with Football Fest Aug. 8 at Lumen Field.

Landed a 4-star cornerback commitment, the class's highest-rated pledge to date, while still chasing a second corner and O-line help. RB Jordan Washington is targeting a late-July return from a spring injury ahead of fall camp. Season opens Sept. 5 vs. Washington State (Apple Cup).

Danny Sprinkle is rebuilding through the transfer portal and overseas recruiting after losing Zoom Diallo to the portal. F Hannes Steinbach, taken 14th overall by Charlotte in the 2026 NBA Draft, remains the program's top recent NBA export.

deepDive.title: When the Number That Cooled Inflation Is the Same Number Now Spiking Again
content: June's CPI report looked like unambiguous good news: headline inflation fell to 3.5% year-over-year from 4.2% in May, and the market rewarded it with a 0.36% S&P gain, a 2-basis-point drop in the 10-year yield, and an 84.5% probability the Fed holds rates this month. But the report's own internals tell a more fragile story — a 5.7% drop in energy prices, powered by a 9.7% collapse in gasoline, did nearly all the work while core CPI barely budged. That's a problem, because the same day the CPI print landed, WTI jumped roughly 2.4% on renewed US-Iran conflict and a threatened Strait of Hormuz blockade. The disinflation narrative markets just priced in was built substantially on the one input now reversing in real time.

Energy flows into CPI two ways, on two different clocks. The direct channel is fast: gasoline and household energy carry roughly a 7% weight in the CPI basket and reprice within days of a crude move, since retail pump prices track futures with only a one-to-three-week lag for refining and distribution. The indirect channel is slower and stickier: higher crude raises input costs for trucking, plastics, fertilizer, and air travel, which shows up in core goods and services over the following two to four months as businesses pass costs through at their own pace. So even if oil settles back down next week, a sustained spike embeds itself into core inflation well after the headline crude story has left the news cycle.

The Fed's own doctrine for handling this is called 'looking through' a supply shock — treating a price spike as transitory if it stems from a one-off disruption rather than broad demand, and not tightening policy in response to it. The doctrine has a mixed track record. After Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, oil roughly doubled in three months and the Fed largely looked through it, correctly, as the shock faded within a year. In 2022, the Fed initially treated the Russia-Ukraine energy spike the same way and got burned — the pass-through proved far stickier than the 1990 episode, forcing the most aggressive hiking cycle in four decades once officials realized core inflation wasn't retreating on its own.

That history is the reason today's 84.5% Fed-hold pricing deserves skepticism rather than acceptance. If the Hormuz standoff drags into August, the July CPI report — due roughly a month from now — could show energy adding back to headline inflation just as June's print showed it subtracting. A Fed that holds this month partly because of a gasoline-driven disinflation reading could find itself reversing that read within one or two reports, which is exactly the kind of whipsaw that moves the front end of the yield curve fast. The 2-year note, which reacts more to near-term Fed expectations than the 10-year, is the instrument to watch if Hormuz tensions don't de-escalate soon.
